title: Year of the Dog
full_review:
"Year of the Dog" (Paramount Vantage) is a quirky tale -- by turns, wryly amusing, sad and thought-provoking -- about lonely office worker Peggy (Molly Shannon) whose beagle Pencil, the focal point of her life, dies mysteriously after wandering one night into the yard of her neighbor Al (John C. Reilly).

The pooch's demise leaves her bereft.

At work, her romantically minded best friend, Layla (Regina King), hopes Peggy will find a fulfilling human relationship, and is thrilled when construction worker Al asks Peggy on a date. But that would-be relationship quickly sours when Peggy learns of Al's passion for hunting, and comes to suspect that Pencil may have ingested a toxic substance in Al's garage.

While she spurns Al's advances, she takes a definite shine to sweet-natured but romantically reticent (and possibly gay) Newt (Peter Sarsgaard), a New Agey animal rights activist who witnessed her grief over Pencil, and thinks she'd be the perfect match for an abused mutt. She reluctantly adopts the large and ornery dog and, like Newt, hones her social conscience about abused animals and becomes a vegan.

Her brother Pier (Tom McCarthy) and sister-in-law Bret (Laura Dern) observe Peggy's transformation with alarm, especially after she almost takes her little niece to view the "holocaust" going on at a local slaughterhouse, and at work Peggy's humorously neurotic boss, Robin (Josh Pais), begins to lose patience as Peggy brings her activism into the office environment.

We won't reveal how it all turns out, but writer-director Mike White's low-keyed comedy avoids the predictable as it explores the validity of its heroine's increasing obsessions with dogs and animal rights, both poking fun at and validating her choices. A compassionate worldview informs the whole film. No character behaves in a mean-spirited way, even as the increasingly zealous Peggy gives them good cause.

Shannon is completely convincing in her obsessive role, but all the performances are finely etched. Though not riotously funny, this gentle comedy stays with you.

The film contains brief innuendo and sexual banter and mild profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
